Volume 10 · Chapter 04

Credit risk and recovery

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v10-c03

By the endValue defaultable claims and separate hazard, recovery and liquidity assumptions.

Price a defaultable claim by its actual payments

Capability. Value finite structural and default-time claims, derive survival from conditional hazards, implement absorbing credit transitions, and explain why recovery timing, dependence and liquidity assumptions matter. The prerequisite is term-structure models and pricing probabilities. We also use positive state prices, ordinary integration and conditional probability. Every stochastic calculation here is finite or uses a stipulated deterministic hazard. No diffusion, Itô lemma or Black–Scholes formula is assumed.

A note promises 100 CU but trades below a matched default-free note. Does the difference reveal a probability of default? Only after specifying what happens on default, when creditors receive money, which probability law prices the claim and what other features affect the quote. A 40% recovery payable immediately is a different asset from a 40% recovery payable years later. A bond's promised yield is also different from its expected return.

Fenwick Credit Desk's examples are original synthetic contracts. Time is measured in years after 1 January 2027; date 0 is before every payout. All claims use one fictional currency, CU, with no taxes, optional calls, collateral changes, fees or other claims except where expressly introduced. Supplied discount factors describe a matched default-free funding environment. The priority and recovery clauses are fictional agreements, not statements of insolvency law. A state labeled default terminates the original promise and replaces it with exactly the specified recovery right.

1. What a credit spread compares

Let a zero-coupon claim promise face F at T, have price B and be compared with a default-free discount factor D(0,T). Its promised continuously compounded yield is y = −log(B/F)/T. The corresponding default-free spot rate is r = −log D(0,T)/T, so the quoted spread is s = −log[B/(FD(0,T))]/T. This definition uses promised face even when the actual receipt is lower or earlier. A coupon bond's YTM is instead a root for its whole promised schedule; subtracting two YTMs need not isolate credit risk if maturity, coupon or optionality differs. A constant spread added to an entire discount curve is another convention, requiring its own price equation.

Separate four ideas: physical expected loss; compensation for losses in costly states; the recovery contract; and a possible liquidity or other nondefault valuation component. The physical law P describes modeled frequencies. A pricing law Q, together with discounting, values state-contingent cash. Q need not equal P and is not an investor's forecast. The Han–Zhou study's March 2008 manuscript illustrates that a measured nondefault component depends on benchmark and estimation choices. We use that dated methodological lesson, not a current empirical decomposition or claim that a spread residual is purely liquidity.

Before comparing quotes, match currency, payment dates, seniority, collateral, tax and embedded-option treatment. Establish whether each price is executable and what funding and short-sale rights exist. A liquidity discount below a theoretical credit value is not a free second price for a perfectly replicable claim in an unrestricted market: either the benchmark is a model value or the relevant friction prevents the proposed arbitrage. Our later liquidity example explicitly has that limited interpretation.

2. Structural debt and equity without an option formula

Consider one nonrecourse debt with face F, no interim distributions, no competing claims and no default before T. Let VT ≥ 0 be available asset cash at maturity, with no liquidation cost in this first contract. If VT ≥ F, creditors receive F and equity receives VT − F. If VT < F, creditors take the available assets and equity receives zero. Equality means full payment with zero equity; whether a different legal definition labels that event default does not alter the cash identity.

Debt payoff HD = min(VT,F) = F − (F − VT)+.
Equity payoff HE = (VT − F)+.
HD + HE = VT, where x+ = max(x,0).

The identities follow by the two cases, not by an option-pricing theorem. In finite states s with positive pricing probabilities Qs and deterministic D, state prices are qs = DQs. Thus B = ΣqsHD,s, E = ΣqsHE,s and B + E = ΣqsVT,s. Given a valid state-price rule this is consistent pricing; if observed assets do not uniquely determine that rule, no arbitrage alone need not identify the supplied Q.

The terminal allocation and importance of indenture restrictions are central to Merton's 1974 structural-credit paper. Its continuous trading and diffusion valuation machinery requires additional assumptions. We use our own finite state prices and derive the payoff allocation locally. Early cash exhaustion, coupon default, restructuring bargaining and other senior claims would require an enlarged contract; they cannot be hidden inside the two-payoff identity.

Worked example 1 — Fenwick's promised yield and actual expectation

One-year asset cash, probabilities and allocated receipts
StateVTPQDebt F = 100Equity
Low700.10.2700
Middle1100.60.510010
High1600.30.310060

With D = 0.96, positive state prices are (0.192, 0.48, 0.288). Debt value is 0.96(14 + 50 + 30) = 90.24; equity is 0.96(5 + 18) = 22.08. Asset value is 0.96(14 + 55 + 48) = 112.32, exactly their sum. Physical default probability is 0.1; pricing default probability is 0.2. Recovery in the sole default state is 70% of face, but that fraction is not the price return.

The physical expected debt receipt is 7 + 60 + 30 = 97, so physical expected return is 97/90.24 − 1 ≈ 7.491135%. Promised simple yield is 100/90.24 − 1 ≈ 10.815603%, versus safe return 1/0.96 − 1 ≈ 4.166667%. Here the simple promised spread decomposes exactly into (100 − 97)/90.24 plus [97/90.24 − 1/0.96], each about 3.324468 percentage points. Expected loss of 3 CU is 3% of face, not the whole spread. The continuously compounded promised spread is −log(0.94) ≈ 6.187540% per year; do not combine this with simple-yield components without converting conventions.

Risk and transfer. For fixed F, min(v,F) is concave and (v − F)+ is convex. A mean-preserving spread under the pricing law can reduce debt value and increase equity value while leaving total asset value unchanged. This is a distributional consequence of the contract, not an operating gain. Keeping only a physical mean unchanged does not by itself keep the priced asset mean unchanged. If a workout consumes resources, allocated claims sum to assets less those costs, so the no-cost value identity must be amended.

3. Conditional hazard, survival and dated recovery

At discrete payment dates 0 = t0 < t1 < … < tn, define hk = Q(default in interval k | alive at tk−1). Let S0 = 1 and Sk = Q(alive at tk). Conditional probability gives Sk = Sk−1(1 − hk), hence Sk = ∏j≤k(1 − hj). Marginal first-default probability is mk = Sk−1hk = Sk−1 − Sk. Their sum is 1 − Sn. Adding conditional hazards treats different at-risk populations as if they were identical.

The same recursions apply under P, using physical conditional hazards. They do not license replacing Q with an estimated physical transition frequency in a price. If Sk−1 = 0, no one remains at risk; the next conditional hazard is undefined rather than a new cohort default rate. A conditional hazard of one exhausts the surviving population. The compact scheduled lab restricts hazards to less than one so its equivalent finite intensity remains defined; the migration lab handles exhausted survival explicitly.

Suppose the coupon amount Ck is paid only if the issuer survives date k, a first default occurs just before that date's coupon, and creditors immediately receive ρkF at that interval end instead of all remaining claims. With deterministic discount factors and recoveries,

B = Σk=1…nD(0,tk)[CkSk + ρkF mk] + D(0,T)F Sn.

These mutually exclusive cash events prevent a default-date coupon or second recovery being paid by accident. Random recovery instead requires Q-weighted conditional recovery in each default event; a physical average is not automatically the right input. If interest rates are stochastic and related to default, use the joint expectation of path discount times cash. Factoring it into today's discount curve times an unconditional survival probability requires additional independence or a suitable change of pricing measure; it is not generally valid.

Worked example 2 — The same 40 CU, at different dates

A three-year Fenwick note promises coupons 6 and face 100. Default-free factors are Dk = (25/26)k, a 4% effective annual rate. Supplied Q hazards are (0.02, 0.03, 0.04); P hazards are separately (0.01, 0.02, 0.03). Recovery is 40 CU, paid at the first interval-end default before the coupon; all future claims then vanish.

Discount the row sums to obtain 3519809/35152 ≈ 100.131116295 CU. The price above face reflects the 6-CU coupon relative to the supplied funding curve; it is not evidence of no default risk. Now change only the recovery contract: every first default still terminates coupons, but the 40 CU is irrevocably owed and paid at year 3, with no additional recovery-counterparty risk. Price becomes 3516299/35152 ≈ 100.031264224. The difference is 40[m1(D1 − D3) + m2(D2 − D3)] = 135/1352 ≈ 0.099852071. Recovery percentage alone did not define a unique value.

4. Continuous survival with ordinary calculus

In a deterministic continuous-time hazard model, let τ be default time and λ(t) ≥ 0 satisfy Q(t < τ ≤ t + Δ | τ > t) = λ(t)Δ + o(Δ). Assume a sufficiently regular survival function S with S(0) = 1 and no initial default atom. Then S(t + Δ) − S(t) = −S(t)λ(t)Δ + o(Δ), so S′(t) = −λ(t)S(t). Integrating d log S/dt = −λ gives S(t) = exp[−∫0tλ(u)du]. This is a deterministic hazard derivation, not a proof for arbitrary stochastic intensities. Constant λ gives S(t) = e−λt, default density λe−λt and conditional default over length Δ equal to 1 − e−λΔ. The approximation λΔ is only first order.

Conversely, an interval conditional probability h < 1 is matched by λ = −log(1 − h)/Δ if a constant intensity within that interval is an appropriate interpolation. The grid probabilities do not identify a unique within-interval default process. Units matter: h is dimensionless over an interval, λ is per year, and S(T) is a cumulative survival probability. Distinct λP and λQ can describe the same default event under different equivalent measures.

With constant deterministic short rate r, constant pricing intensity λ, face F and recovery fraction ρ, a zero-coupon claim that pays ρF at default has price

Bpar = F e−(r+λ)T + ρF∫0Tλe−(r+λ)tdt
= F[e−(r+λ)T + ρλ(1 − e−(r+λ)T)/(r + λ)], when r + λ ≠ 0.

The first term prices survival principal; the second integrates discounted recovery against first-default density. If r + λ = 0 the integral equals λT, so Bpar = F(1 + ρλT); this can occur with a negative short rate and needs no division by zero. If λ = 0, price is Fe−rT. If ρ = 0, it is Fe−(r+λ)T. A delayed contract paying ρF at T after any prior default instead has Bdelayed = Fe−rT[ρ + (1 − ρ)e−λT]. With r ≥ 0, immediate recovery is at least as valuable; negative rates can reverse the timing advantage.

A third contract pays a fraction ρ of the claim's pre-default market value at default. This is not a fraction of face or of the default-free claim. Under constant coefficients, let b(t) be its pre-default value, with b(T) = F. The short-step pricing relation is b(t) = e−rΔ[(1 − λΔ)b(t + Δ) + λΔρb(t + Δ)] + o(Δ). Expansion gives b′(t) = [r + λ(1 − ρ)]b(t), hence Bmarket = Fe−[r+λ(1−ρ)]T. Thus s = λ(1 − ρ) is exact for this specific recovery-of-market-value contract with constant coefficients. For immediate recovery of par it is generally a short-maturity approximation, derived by expanding B/F = 1 − [r + λ(1 − ρ)]T + o(T).

Duffie's preliminary August 1998 manuscript explicitly distinguishes recovery bases and discrete versus simultaneous recovery. Our elementary constant-coefficient formulas follow directly from the stated cash contracts. The manuscript's more general stochastic-intensity results need regularity and dependence assumptions beyond this chapter; its discussion of possible recovery practices is not a statement of current law.

Worked example 3 — Three recovery contracts, three prices

Take F = 100, T = 5 years, r = 0.03, λQ = 0.06, λP = 0.02 and ρ = 0.4. Pricing survival is e−0.3 ≈ 0.740818221, while physical survival is e−0.1 ≈ 0.904837418. The distinction is stipulated; one cannot estimate the latter by reading the former from a price.

Immediate recovery of par gives 100[e−0.45 + (0.024/0.09)(1 − e−0.45)] = 73.4260644523. Maturity-paid recovery gives 100e−0.15[0.4 + 0.6e−0.3] = 72.6860081543. Recovery of pre-default market value gives 100e−0.33 = 71.8923733432. All use the same intensity and displayed fraction, but different recovery amounts or dates. The immediate-par spread is about 3.177824237% per year, whereas λ(1 − ρ) = 3.6% exactly describes the third contract. Substituting 3.6% into the first contract changes the instrument.

5. Migration and first passage into default

A finite transition matrix T has nonnegative rows summing to one. For states A, B and D, Tij is the conditional next-period probability of state j given current state i. D is absorbing: its row is (0,0,1). For an initial row distribution eA, the distribution n periods later is eATn. This follows by conditioning once and then induction; time-homogeneous multiplication assumes the same matrix applies at every step and that the current state contains the information needed for the next transition. Time-varying matrices require their ordered product.

If Fn is the D entry after n steps, first default in period n has probability Fn − Fn−1. Because D is absorbing, this difference counts each default once. Paying recovery on every later occupancy of D would create claims that the contract extinguished. P matrices describe risk frequencies conditional on the modeled state. Q matrices price cash under the stipulated discounting. A fitted historical matrix is not automatically a pricing matrix, nor does a rating label prove homogeneity, stable transition probabilities or adequate data at the horizon.

Worked example 4 — Migration changes the horizon hazard

For a separate annual Fenwick credit model, rows and columns are A, B, D. Let TQ = [[0.85,0.12,0.03], [0.10,0.80,0.10], [0,0,1]] and TP = [[0.90,0.09,0.01], [0.15,0.80,0.05], [0,0,1]]. Start in A. These matrices share support but have different probabilities.

6. Dependence changes who bears the tail

For default indicators I1, I2 with marginal probabilities p1, p2, let j be their joint default probability. The four probabilities are 1 − p1 − p2 + j, p1 − j, p2 − j and j. Nonnegativity is equivalent to max(0,p1 + p2 − 1) ≤ j ≤ min(p1,p2), the two-event Fréchet bounds. Therefore a requested correlation may be infeasible even if it lies in [−1,1]. With nondegenerate marginals, correlation is [j − p1p2]/√[p1(1 − p1)p2(1 − p2)]. If either marginal is 0 or 1, the correlation denominator vanishes.

With fixed loss amounts L1, L2, pool loss is L = L1I1 + L2I2. Its mean uses only marginals, but variance includes 2L1L2(j − p1p2). A tranche absorbs losses only between its attachment a and detachment b, so its loss is min(max(L − a,0),b − a). This nonlinear allocation makes the joint law relevant even when total expected loss is unchanged. Correlation alone is generally insufficient for larger portfolios; many multivariate joint laws can share the same pairwise correlations.

Worked example 5 — Equal pool loss, different senior loss

Two notes each have face 100 and recovery 40 at one-year settlement. Each defaults with probability 0.1. Compare j = 0.01 (independence) with j = 0.05 (clustering). For this separate pricing illustration only, investors are stipulated risk-neutral, Q = P, and D = 0.96. A junior tranche has principal 60 and absorbs the first 60 of pool loss; a senior tranche has principal 140 and absorbs the next 140. Their payments exhaust the pool's actual receipts.

Original two-name joint laws and loss allocation
Default stateIndependent probabilityClustered probabilityPool lossJunior / senior loss
Neither0.810.8500 / 0
Only first0.090.056060 / 0
Only second0.090.056060 / 0
Both0.010.0512060 / 60

Expected pool loss is 12 in both cases. Variance rises from 648 to 936 CU², and default-indicator correlation rises from 0 to 4/9. Junior expected loss falls from 60(0.19) = 11.4 to 60(0.15) = 9; senior loss rises from 60(0.01) = 0.6 to 60(0.05) = 3. Clustering reduces the chance of any loss but raises the severe-loss probability. It does not make every tranche worse in expected value.

Junior prices are 0.96(60 − 11.4) = 46.656 and 0.96(60 − 9) = 48.96; senior prices are 133.824 and 131.52. Both sums equal 0.96(200 − 12) = 180.48. These prices rely on the expressly supplied Q = P condition. A real physical loss table alone would support a risk calculation, not those prices.

7. One quote does not identify three mechanisms

For a zero-coupon face F with constant recovery ρ paid at maturity after any default, define q = Q(τ ≤ T). With deterministic discount D, B = FD[1 − (1 − ρ)q]. A price ratio x = B/(FD) identifies the product (1 − ρ)q, not its factors. When ρ < 1, q = (1 − x)/(1 − ρ) is a conditional calibration only if it lies in [0,1]. A finite constant intensity requires q < 1 and λ = −log(1 − q)/T. At ρ = 1 the maturity cash is F irrespective of default: x = 1 leaves hazard unidentified, and x ≠ 1 is incompatible with this frictionless contract.

For F = 100, T = 2, D = 0.9 and price 85.5, x = 0.95. Recovery/default pairs (0,0.05), (0.5,0.10) and (0.75,0.20) all price the same note. Their constant Q intensities are about 0.025646647, 0.052680258 and 0.111571776 per year. No physical default probability has been supplied or inferred. If instead an assumed illiquidity price multiplier 95/97 relates the observed price to a nonreplicable credit benchmark, that benchmark ratio is 0.97. With ρ = 0.5, q becomes 0.06 and λ ≈ 0.030937702. The wedge is a modeling premise, not a separately observed causal fact.

More maturities, recovery-linked claims, defensible recovery evidence and reliable liquidity measurements can restrict the alternatives, but each adds information or assumptions. The same logic applies when default and recovery co-vary: pricing needs the appropriate joint or conditional expectation, not a product of unrelated averages. An empirical critique should examine the recovery basis/date, benchmark curve, matched cash flows, inclusion and revision rules, identification of P versus Q, and whether a claimed nondefault component also captures model error or omitted features.

8. Reproduce and challenge the contracts

Download the original contract register, standard-library lab, complete reference result, four-file manifest and execution/model guide. Run python3 v10-c04-analysis.py; use --input copy.json --output result.json for a separate intervention. Import and run(data) are quiet; no network or installation is needed. Finite results are exact rational strings, exponentials/logarithms are labeled approximations, and undefined quantities are JSON null.

The bounded lab prices each explicit contract, reports P and Q separately, preserves every cash row, compounds migration, reconciles all tranche receipts and retains the entire calibration grid. It validates common P/Q support, nonnegative probabilities, absorbing default, positive discount factors, recovery fractions and schedule lengths. Negative rates are allowed within finite bounds. Intervene by adding a 10% workout cost in structural default states, delaying recovery, exhausting live migration at the first step, changing only physical probabilities, or moving joint default to a feasible boundary. Explain which prices should change before running the edit. A passed calculation is conditional on its inputs, not evidence that the model forecasts default.

Exercises

Show dates, units, probability measure and claim closure in every answer. Decimal prices may be rounded to six places after deriving the exact expression. In proof questions, state the assumptions that make the result true. The final critique is assessed by the explicit criteria in its solution.

  1. Change leverage while preserving the asset law. Keep Worked example 1's assets, P, Q and discount factor, but raise the sole debt face to 120. Compute state debt/equity receipts, each price, both default probabilities, physical expected debt receipt and return, promised simple yield and the continuous promised spread. Explain why raising face did not create asset value.
  2. Prove and calculate a risk transfer. Return to face 100 and no costs. Split the middle asset state 110 into equally likely conditional outcomes 80 and 140 under Q, leaving its total Q mass 0.5 and all other states unchanged. Calculate asset, debt and equity prices before/after and the new pricing default probability. Prove that for any nonnegative finite random asset cash X and face F, replacing a fixed conditional value EQ[X | branch] by X weakly lowers conditional expected debt payoff and weakly raises equity payoff. Identify a condition for strictness and explain why preserving only a physical mean is insufficient for the price claim.
  3. Write the recovery ledger. A new two-year note has face 100, coupon 4 at each year end, pricing hazards 0.05 and 0.10, discount factors 0.95 and 0.90, and recovery 30. Default occurs at an end date before its coupon; all remaining rights terminate. Compute survival, first-default mass, each expected cash item and price. Reprice when the same 30 is instead paid at year 2 after either default, without further risk. Explain the exact timing difference and why a default-year coupon cannot be added.
  4. Invert survival and prove the recursion. Supplied Q survivals at years 0–3 are (1,0.96,0.90,0.81). Recover each conditional and marginal default probability and its equivalent within-year constant intensity. Derive the product survival formula by conditioning and the exponential formula for a differentiable deterministic hazard. Compare the sum of conditional hazards with the three-year default probability. What becomes undefined if a supplied survival reaches zero, and what pattern makes a claimed survival curve impossible?
  5. Integrate recovery instead of shifting a yield. A four-year zero-coupon face 100 has r = 0.02, λQ = 0.05 and ρ = 0.4. Derive its immediate-par-recovery price by integrating the default-time density. Compute the maturity-paid-recovery comparison. Derive the r + λ = 0 limit and evaluate it at r = −0.05, λ = 0.05, T = 4. State the λ = 0 limit and why no division by a nearly zero number is necessary in a careful implementation.
  6. Full recovery is not a complete timing description. A two-year zero-coupon face 100 has r = 0.04, λQ = 0.10 and ρ = 1. Compare immediate recovery of par with recovery of pre-default market value. Derive the latter's backward ordinary differential equation from one short pricing step. Compute both prices and the immediate-par promised spread. Explain how that spread can be negative without creating an arbitrage or increasing the promised face.
  7. Migration, repricing and absorption. Start the Worked example 4 pricing matrix in B and use only two years, with D1 = 25/26, D2 = (25/26)², face 100, no coupons and recovery 40 on first default. Find the first and second default masses, survival and price. Independently reproduce the price by one-step backward valuation using the remaining one-year values conditional on being A or B. Quantify the price change caused by a year-1 A-to-B downgrade of an otherwise identical one-year remaining claim. Explain what double-counting an absorbing D balance would do.
  8. Unequal marginals constrain correlation. Two one-year face-100 notes recover 40; their physical default marginals are 0.1 and 0.2. Derive the feasible joint-probability and correlation ranges. Compare independence with joint default 0.04: full state table, pool expected loss and variance, probability loss exceeds 60, and expected losses of the first-60 junior and remaining-140 senior tranches. For a separate stipulated pricing comparison, take Q = P and D = 0.95 and price both tranches at joint default 0.04. Explain why this extra pricing assumption was needed.
  9. Construct observationally equivalent calibrations. A two-year face-100 zero note has D = 0.9 and price 81. All default recoveries are paid at maturity without further risk. First set liquidity multiplier to one and find q and constant λQ for recoveries 0.4 and 0.6. Then set recovery 0.4 and the observed-to-credit price multiplier to 18/19. Reprice every alternative exactly. Discuss the recovery-1 boundary and identify what additional evidence could help separate default intensity, recovery and liquidity without pretending that physical and pricing probabilities are identical.
  10. Research and model critique. An analyst estimates a historical migration matrix, observes a bond spread and concludes: “The default probability is spread divided by one minus average recovery; this is uniquely data-identified. Recovery is 40% of face, so I can discount every promise at r + 0.6λ. If correlation rises, every tranche becomes less valuable. Any remaining spread is liquidity.” Assess each claim using the chapter's derivations and at least two of its primary-source scopes. Supply one numerical counterexample from a solved case, distinguish a modeling identity from an empirical finding, and propose a concrete validation protocol addressing contracts, data, measures and out-of-sample use. No current credit quote or legal rule may be invented.
Complete solutions and graduate evaluation criteria

  1. Leverage and promised versus expected returns

    Debt receives (70,110,120), equity (0,0,40). Debt price is 0.96[0.2(70) + 0.5(110) + 0.3(120)] = 100.8; equity is 0.96(12) = 11.52. The sum remains 112.32. Both P and Q default probabilities now equal 0.7 because the low and middle states cannot pay 120; their equality here does not imply that the whole P and Q laws coincide.

    Physical expected receipt is 0.1(70) + 0.6(110) + 0.3(120) = 109, giving expected return 109/100.8 − 1 = 41/504 ≈ 8.134921%. Promised simple yield is 120/100.8 − 1 = 4/21 ≈ 19.047619%. The continuous promised spread is −log[100.8/(120 × 0.96)] = −log(7/8) ≈ 13.353139% per year. Larger face transfers some terminal residual from equity to debt without changing V or its state prices. It does not supply new assets in this comparison; a real new debt issue with cash proceeds would require a different asset balance.

  2. A conditional convexity proof

    The four asset outcomes are (70,80,140,160), with Q = (0.2,0.25,0.25,0.3). Their Q mean is still 117 and price still 112.32. Debt's Q mean is 14 + 20 + 25 + 30 = 89, price 85.44; equity mean is 0 + 0 + 10 + 18 = 28, price 26.88. Relative to the original, debt loses 4.8, equity gains 4.8, and pricing default probability rises to 0.45. A higher equity value alone is not a higher total firm value.

    For an elementary proof let μ = EQ[X | branch]. If μ ≤ F, then min(X,F) ≤ X state by state, so E[min(X,F) | branch] ≤ μ = min(μ,F). If μ ≥ F, min(X,F) ≤ F, so the same inequality holds. Subtract this debt inequality from E[X | branch] = μ to get E[(X − F)+ | branch] ≥ (μ − F)+. Positive conditional mass strictly below and strictly above F makes the inequality strict: if μ ≤ F, some X is truncated above F; if μ ≥ F, some min(X,F) lies strictly below F. If the whole branch stays on one side, the payoff is linear there and equality can hold. This is a pricing-law mean-preserving comparison. A P-mean-preserving change can alter the Q mean and total price, so it need not be a pure transfer.

  3. Two-year cash reconciliation

    S1 = 0.95 and S2 = 0.95 × 0.90 = 0.855. First-default masses are 0.05 and 0.095; together with final survival they sum to one. At year 1, expected coupon is 4(0.95) = 3.8 and recovery is 30(0.05) = 1.5, giving PV 0.95(5.3) = 5.035. At year 2, expected coupon is 3.42, principal 85.5 and recovery 2.85; their PV is 0.90(91.77) = 82.593. Total price is 87.628.

    Moving the first year's 1.5 expected recovery to year 2 reduces value by 1.5(0.95 − 0.90) = 0.075, giving 87.553. Nothing else changes. Paying the coupon to a newly defaulted name contradicts the before-coupon trigger. Paying the coupon after default in a later period also preserves a claim that the contract terminated.

  4. Population at risk and a differential limit

    Conditional hazards are 1 − 0.96 = 0.04, 1 − 0.90/0.96 = 0.0625, and 1 − 0.81/0.90 = 0.10. Marginal masses are 0.04, 0.06, 0.09, totaling 0.19. Equivalent annual intensities are −log(0.96) ≈ 0.040821995, −log(0.9375) ≈ 0.064538521 and −log(0.90) ≈ 0.105360516. Their sum is −log(0.81), but the sum of conditional hazards is 0.2025, not default probability 0.19.

    Conditioning gives Q(alive at tk) = Q(alive at tk−1)Q(alive at tk | alive at tk−1); induction proves the product. With S differentiable and a deterministic continuous hazard as defined in the text, S′ = −λS; integrating while S > 0 gives log S(t) − log S(0) = −∫λ and therefore the exponential formula. Finite integrable hazard cannot produce S = 0 at a finite horizon. In a discrete model, after survival reaches zero, later conditional probabilities on survival are undefined; subsequent marginal defaults must be zero. Survival must begin at one, remain in [0,1] and be nonincreasing. An upward step cannot be repaired by a negative default hazard.

  5. Recovery integration and the removable singularity

    Under Q, first-default density is 0.05e−0.05t. Discount the 40-CU recovery at t and add survival principal: B = 100e−0.28 + 40∫040.05e−0.07tdt = 100[e−0.28 + (2/7)(1 − e−0.28)] ≈ 82.555981533. Maturity recovery instead gives 100e−0.08[0.4 + 0.6e−0.20] ≈ 82.271678343. Positive discounting makes the earlier recovery more valuable by about 0.284303190 CU.

    For k = r + λ, (1 − e−kT)/k tends to T, by the derivative of the exponential at zero or directly from ∫0Te−ktdt. At r = −0.05 and λ = 0.05, survival-discounted principal is 100 and recovery PV is 100(0.4)(0.05)(4) = 8, so price is 108. Negative r makes the safe price 100e0.2, which is larger still. At λ = 0, no recovery event occurs and price is 100e−rT. Implement k = 0 by its limit and small nonzero k with expm1 or a controlled equivalent expression, preserving finite outputs rather than dividing two badly rounded small numbers.

  6. Full par recovery accelerates a payment

    Let b(t) be pre-default value. Conditional on being alive, one short step gives b(t) = (1 − rΔ)[(1 − λΔ)b(t + Δ) + λΔρb(t + Δ)] + o(Δ). With b(t + Δ) = b(t) + b′(t)Δ + o(Δ), cancellation gives b′(t) = [r + λ(1 − ρ)]b(t). Terminal condition b(T) = 100 implies b(0) = 100e−[r+λ(1−ρ)]T. This uses a precisely stated fraction of market value and ordinary differentiability, not a fraction-of-face substitute.

    At ρ = 1, market-value recovery gives the safe price 100e−0.08 ≈ 92.311634639. Immediate par recovery instead gives 100[e−0.28 + (5/7)(1 − e−0.28)] ≈ 93.022392613. Its promised spread is −log(93.022392613/100)/2 − 0.04 ≈ −0.003835029 per year, about −38.350295 basis points. Earlier payment of all 100 is valuable at positive rates; its cash flow differs from receiving 100 only at year 2. Equal face is not equal dated payoff, so no law-of-one-price violation follows. The example refutes a universal monotonic assertion about hazard and price under arbitrary recovery timing.

  7. Two ways to price a migrating claim

    Starting in B, first default probability is 0.10. Second-period first default is 0.10(0.03) + 0.80(0.10) = 0.083; cumulative default is 0.183 and final survival 0.817. Direct value is 40(0.10)D1 + [40(0.083) + 100(0.817)]D2 = 8575/104 ≈ 82.451923077.

    With one year remaining, state A value is (25/26)[0.03(40) + 0.97(100)] = 2455/26 ≈ 94.423076923. State B value is (25/26)[0.10(40) + 0.90(100)] = 1175/13 ≈ 90.384615385. At date 0, backward pricing from B gives (25/26)[0.10(40) + 0.10(2455/26) + 0.80(1175/13)] = 8575/104, matching the first-default calculation. A downgrade from A to B changes the live one-year claim value by −105/26 ≈ −4.038461538. This is conditional repricing under fixed assumptions, not a forecast of migration.

    At first entry to D, 40 is paid and the note has no remaining value. Paying 40 again on the previously defaulted 0.10 mass at year 2 overvalues the note by 40(0.10)D2. An absorbing state records history; it does not authorize recurring cash.

  8. Fréchet bounds and a senior tail

    The feasible joint range is 0 ≤ j ≤ 0.1. The correlation denominator is √(0.1 × 0.9 × 0.2 × 0.8) = 0.12, so correlation ranges from −1/6 to 2/3. Joint 0.04 has correlation 1/6; independence has j = 0.02 and correlation zero. The four probabilities (neither, first only, second only, both) are (0.72,0.08,0.18,0.02) under independence and (0.74,0.06,0.16,0.04) under the alternative. Every entry is nonnegative and both marginals reconcile.

    Expected pool loss is 60(0.1 + 0.2) = 18 in either law. Variance is 60²[0.1(0.9) + 0.2(0.8) + 2(j − 0.02)], equal to 900 under independence and 1044 at j = 0.04. Loss exceeds 60 only if both default, so its probability doubles from 0.02 to 0.04. Junior expected losses are 60(0.30 − j), namely 16.8 and 15.6; senior losses are 60j, namely 1.2 and 2.4. Their sums remain 18.

    Only with the additional Q = P pricing stipulation and D = 0.95 do alternative-law prices become junior 0.95(60 − 15.6) = 42.18 and senior 0.95(140 − 2.4) = 130.72. Total 172.9 equals 0.95(200 − 18). Physical correlation and losses alone do not reveal how investors price state cash, so without that stipulation these are expectations rather than unique claim values.

  9. A price fits multiple models

    The observed ratio is 81/(100 × 0.9) = 0.9. With ρ = 0.4 and no wedge, q = 0.1/0.6 = 1/6, λ = −log(5/6)/2 ≈ 0.091160778. With ρ = 0.6, q = 0.1/0.4 = 1/4, λ = −log(3/4)/2 ≈ 0.143841036. Each reprices exactly to 90[1 − (1 − ρ)q] = 81.

    With multiplier 18/19, the modeled credit value is 81 × 19/18 = 85.5, a ratio 0.95. At ρ = 0.4 this means q = 0.05/0.6 = 1/12 and λ = −log(11/12)/2 ≈ 0.043505688. Repricing gives 90[1 − (3/5)(1/12)](18/19) = 81. The multiplier describes a supplied frictional or nonreplicable model benchmark; no unrestricted duplicate-asset arbitrage is assumed away without disclosure.

    At recovery one and maturity payment, credit cash is always 100: without a wedge its value must be 90 and the observed 81 is incompatible. If a wedge of 0.9 were independently justified, every hazard would fit; hazard is then unidentified. Better evidence could include matched maturity prices, contracts that vary recovery exposure, recovery amounts and payment dates from comparable completed cases, defensible execution/liquidity observations, and a separately estimated physical frequency model with uncertainty. Each source needs selection and measurement checks. Extra assumptions can identify a conditional model; they do not turn a single price into uniquely observed default probability.

  10. Critique protocol and scoring criteria

    The analyst first confuses a promised spread, a per-year intensity and a cumulative physical probability. Even where s = λQ(1 − ρ) is exact, it identifies a pricing mean-loss rate under a specific recovery convention; Q(τ ≤ T) = 1 − e−λQT is another quantity, and λP need not equal λQ. A historical migration matrix also requires a time-homogeneous state model before powers give horizon frequencies. Second, a 40%-of-face clause does not supply recovery of pre-default market value. Worked example 3 has the same intensity and fraction but prices 73.426064452 and 71.892373343 for those different contracts. Third, Exercise 9 gives three conditional calibrations for the same quote, refuting unique identification.

    The tranche assertion fails because the junior loss function saturates. Worked example 5 raises senior expected loss from 0.6 to 3 while reducing junior loss from 11.4 to 9; total expected pool loss remains 12. Last, a residual between a quoted spread and a model-implied credit component can contain recovery errors, benchmark mismatch, option or tax differences, selection effects and other omitted features as well as liquidity. A descriptive residual is not a causal estimate of an isolated mechanism.

    The scoped primary comparison should explain that Merton's terminal allocation rests on stated indenture and modeling assumptions; its diffusion formula cannot be inserted without its prerequisites. Duffie's dated manuscript distinguishes recovery bases and dates, supporting the need to price the stipulated contract. Han and Zhou use matched cash-flow and CDS-based modeling choices and compare benchmark curves; their historical method does not make every residual universal liquidity. No source is treated as proof of the synthetic inputs.

    A concrete protocol preserves raw price timestamps, inclusion rules and debt terms; reconciles currency, seniority, collateral, coupons and payment dates; specifies recovery base and settlement delay; estimates P frequencies separately from Q calibration; reports uncertainty and model alternatives; tests absorbing default and every cash identity; compares multiple maturities and recovery assumptions; and evaluates a frozen model on later observations without retuning the earlier forecast. Require independent evidence before labeling a residual causal liquidity or using a tail result in a risk limit.

    Evaluation: full credit requires correct quantity/measure distinctions, a contract-specific recovery correction, a quantitative nonidentification or dependence counterexample, accurate use of at least two scoped primary references, a feasible data/validation protocol, and clear limits on empirical conclusions. A list of general risks without connecting each to the failed inference is insufficient. Reasoned alternative models earn credit when their new assumptions and tests are explicit.

Teach-back and retention

Teach-back. Explain to a colleague why two bonds displaying “40% recovery” and the same hazard can have different prices, and why that hazard may not predict actual default frequencies.

Model answer. The contract must specify 40% of face, market value or another base, and when the recovery is paid. These choices change dated state receipts. The immediate-par and market-value contracts in Worked example 3 price at about 73.4261 and 71.8924 despite the same stated fraction and λQ = 0.06. That intensity belongs to a pricing law; the supplied physical intensity is separately 0.02. A correct explanation identifies both the cash-contract distinction and P/Q distinction, rather than treating every difference as “risk.”

Delayed retention, after 7–14 days. Without the reference output: (i) recover conditional hazard from S1 = 0.9 and S2 = 0.81; (ii) explain why default-state occupancy cannot earn recovery repeatedly; (iii) with equal marginals p, fixed loss L per name and joint j, derive junior first-L and senior remaining loss expectations; (iv) identify the missing information in “spread is 120 basis points, so default probability is 2%.”

Answers. (i) Second-interval hazard is 1 − 0.81/0.9 = 0.1, while its marginal default mass is 0.09. (ii) Recovery is paid on first entry and terminates the original claim; occupancy afterward only remembers the default. (iii) Junior expected loss is L(2p − j), senior expected loss Lj, total 2Lp. (iv) One needs spread convention and maturity, recovery base/date, pricing versus physical measure, benchmark and other contract/friction components. Even the approximation 0.012/(1 − 0.4) = 0.02 is a per-year pricing intensity under additional premises, not an identified cumulative physical probability. Advancement requires all four mechanisms and a fresh transfer in which one recovery date or marginal changes.

Extensions and the boundary of this chapter

The finite and deterministic models establish the cash and probability logic needed for more elaborate credit work. Stochastic intensities correlated with rates, uncertain recovery, contagion, large-portfolio dependence, early structural default and imperfect information demand further modeling and evidence. Stochastic calculus (planned) and continuous-time option valuation (planned) supply later tools; they do not remove contract or identification questions. In practice, a carefully stated small model is more informative than an exact computation attached to an unspecified recovery right.

Sources and further study

  • Robert C. Merton — On the Pricing of Corporate Debt: The Risk Structure of Interest Rates, Journal of Finance 29(2), 449–470 (May 1974) — Primary structural-credit reference for explicit debt indenture restrictions, debt/equity terminal payoffs and limits of applying a structural model. The chapter prices its own finite states rather than importing diffusion or option-pricing formulas.
  • Darrell Duffie — Defaultable Term Structure Models with Fractional Recovery of Par, preliminary author manuscript (18 August 1998) — Primary methodological distinction among recovery of par, default-free value and market value, explicit default/recovery dates, physical versus pricing intensities and survival/recovery payment separation. Constant deterministic-rate formulas are independently derived in the chapter.
  • Song Han and Hao Zhou — Effects of Liquidity on the Nondefault Component of Corporate Yield Spreads: Evidence from Intraday Transactions Data, FEDS 2008-40 (March 2008 manuscript) — Dated primary empirical-method critique: a measured nondefault component depends on benchmark curve, matched cash flows, credit-model/CDS assumptions, sample inclusion and liquidity measurement. No result is asserted as a current or universal spread decomposition.
